Backsliding
BAK-sly-ding
n.
“Back” + “slide”; rendering the Hebrew mēshūbāh (turning back, apostasy) and sārar (to be stubborn, turn away). A sliding back from God in heart and life.

See also: Backsliding

📖 Biblical Definition

Backsliding is the spiritual declension of one who has known the ways of God—a sliding back from former zeal, faith, obedience, and communion into coldness, worldliness, and sin. The term is chiefly an Old Testament one, applied to Israel’s repeated turning away from the LORD: ‘Turn, O backsliding children, saith the LORD’; ‘Their backslidings are increased’; ‘I will heal their backsliding.’ It describes not a single fall but a gradual, often imperceptible decline—the slow cooling of love, the creeping in of worldliness, the neglect of the means of grace, the loss of first love, until the soul that once burned grows cold and distant. A vital distinction must be drawn. The backsliding of a true believer is real and grievous but never total or final: a genuine saint may decline grievously, lose his joy and assurance, grieve the Spirit, and fall into serious sin—as David, as Peter—yet he cannot fall away utterly or finally, for he is kept by the power of God, and the same grace that saved him will recover him, often through the bitter chastening of his own backsliding. This is to be distinguished from the apostasy of the false professor, who, never truly converted, falls away completely and finally, going out from among the people of God because he was never of them. The marks of backsliding include the decay of private devotion, growing love of the world, neglect of the Word and prayer, increasing tolerance of sin, the loss of tenderness of conscience, and a fading delight in spiritual things. Its causes are the deceitfulness of sin, the seductions of the world, the assaults of the enemy, and above all the neglect of the means of grace and the heart’s natural drift from God. Its recovery comes by the renewed working of grace: conviction of one’s declension, humbling and repentance, return to one’s first works, and fresh casting of oneself upon Christ. God’s tender call to the backslider is full of mercy: ‘Return, ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings.’ The believer’s safeguard is watchfulness and diligence in the means of grace, that he may not begin the imperceptible slide; and his comfort, if he has fallen, is that the Shepherd seeks and restores His straying sheep.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BACKSLIDE as to apostatize; to fall off; to turn gradually from the faith and practice of Christianity; and BACKSLIDER as an apostate.

expand to see more

BACKSLIDE, v.i. — To fall off; to apostatize; to turn gradually from the faith and practice of Christianity; to fall from virtue or holiness; to recede.

BACKSLIDING, n. — The act of apostatizing or falling off; a falling off or defection in faith or practice; declension in religion.

📖 Key Scripture

Jeremiah 3:22 — "Return, ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings. Behold, we come unto thee; for thou art the Lord our God."

Hosea 14:4 — "I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him."

Revelation 2:4-5 — "Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love. Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works."

Proverbs 14:14 — "The backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways: and a good man shall be satisfied from himself."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

No major postmodern redefinition, but the doctrine is distorted by confusing the recoverable backsliding of a true saint with the final apostasy of a false professor—either denying that saints can decline, or denying that they are kept from final falling.

expand to see more

The doctrine of backsliding is distorted chiefly by the failure to distinguish the backsliding of a true believer from the apostasy of a false professor. On one side, some so stress the believer’s security that they will not admit a true saint can decline grievously at all, explaining away the real and serious declensions of David, Peter, and many a believer since, and so leaving the backslidden Christian without the warnings and the tender calls to return that Scripture addresses to him. On the other side, some so stress the reality of backsliding that they conclude a true believer may fall away finally and be lost, confusing the grievous-but-recoverable decline of a saint with the total-and-final apostasy of one who was never truly converted. Both err by collapsing a vital distinction.

Scripture holds both truths together. A true believer may backslide grievously—losing his first love, falling into serious sin, grieving the Spirit, forfeiting his joy and assurance, and bringing the bitter chastening of God upon himself—and this is to be taken with the utmost seriousness, warned against, and repented of. Yet such a one cannot fall away utterly or finally, for he is kept by the power of God through faith, and the Good Shepherd will seek and restore His straying sheep, often using the very bitterness of the backsliding to humble and reclaim him. The false professor, by contrast, who falls away completely and never returns, shows thereby that he was never truly of the flock. The recovery of the doctrine restores both the warning and the comfort: the believer is warned to watch against the imperceptible slide, to keep his first love, and to abide in the means of grace; and the backslider is comforted with God’s tender call—‘Return, ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings’—and the assurance that the grace which first saved him is mighty to recover him still.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The doctrine rests on Israel’s mēshūbāh (backsliding, turning away) and the leaving of first love—a real declension the LORD calls the wanderer to return (shūb) from.

Usage

"Backsliding is the gradual declension of one who knew God’s ways—the cooling of love, the creeping in of worldliness."

"A true saint may backslide grievously but never finally; the false professor falls away completely, proving he was never of the flock."

"God’s call to the backslider is full of mercy: ‘Return, ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings.’"
